lines.text: Why do we get goosebumps? We hardly have fur.
lines.phonemes: wˌaɪ dˈuː wiː ɡɛt ɡˈuːsbʌmps? wiː hˈɑːdli hav fˈɜː.

lines.text: Nearly every hair has its own tiny muscle, and when we're cold or frightened, a nerve tugs it, pulling the hair upright and the skin into a bump.
lines.phonemes: nˌiəli ˈɛvɹɪ hˈeə hɐz ɪts ˈəʊn tˈaɪni mˈʌsəl, and wɛn wiə kˈəʊld ɔː fɹˈaɪtənd, ɐ nˈɜːv tˈʌɡz ɪt, pˈʊlɪŋ ðə hˈeəɹ ˈʌpɹaɪt and ðə skˈɪn ˌɪntʊ ɐ bˈʌmp.

lines.text: In a furry animal, that fluffs the coat into a blanket of trapped air. We have about as many hair follicles as a chimpanzee, but ours grow fine, almost invisible hairs.
lines.phonemes: ɪn ɐ fˈɜːɹi ˈanɪməl, ðat flˈʌfs ðə kˈəʊt ˌɪntʊ ɐ blˈaŋkɪt ɒv tɹˈapt ˈeə. wiː hav ɐbˌaʊt az mˈɛni hˈeə fˈɒlɪkəlz az ˈeɪ ʧˌɪmpænzˈiː , bˌʌt aʊəz ɡɹˈəʊ fˈaɪn, ˈɔːlməʊst ɪnvˈɪzɪbəl hˈeəz.

lines.text: So the bumps look like a leftover. But a team at Harvard found that nerve also reaches the stem cells that grow hair, and the muscle holds it in place.
lines.phonemes: sˌəʊ ðə bˈʌmps lˈʊk lˈaɪk ɐ lˈɛftəʊvə. bˌʌt ɐ tˈiːm at hˈɑːvəd fˈaʊnd ðat nˈɜːv ˈɔːlsəʊ ɹˈiːtʃɪz ðə stˈɛm sˈɛlz ðat ɡɹˈəʊ hˈeə, and ðə mˈʌsəl hˈəʊldz ɪt ɪn plˈeɪs.

lines.text: In the cold, that nerve wakes the stem cells, and the mice grew new hair sooner. Take the little muscle away, and the wiring fades.
lines.phonemes: ɪnðə kˈəʊld, ðat nˈɜːv wˈeɪks ðə stˈɛm sˈɛlz, and ðə mˈaɪs ɡɹˈuː njˈuː hˈeə sˈuːnə. tˈeɪk ðə lˈɪtəl mˈʌsəl ɐwˈeɪ, and ðə wˈaɪəɹɪŋ fˈeɪdz.

lines.text: And most of the hairs it tends are thinner than a third of a sheet of paper.
lines.phonemes: and mˈəʊst əv ðə hˈeəz ɪt tˈɛndz ɑː θˈɪnə ðˌanə θˈɜːd əvə ʃˈiːt ɒv pˈeɪpə.

lines.text: So why do we still get goosebumps? Because the muscle that raises a hair still looks after it.
lines.phonemes: sˌəʊ wˌaɪ dˈuː wiː stˈɪl ɡɛt ɡˈuːsbʌmps? bɪkˈɒz ðə mˈʌsəl ðat ɹˈeɪzɪz ɐ hˈeə stˈɪl lˈʊks ˈaftəɹ ɪt.

lines.text: That's the outer layer, for now. Next season, we go deeper.
lines.phonemes: ðats ðɪ ˈaʊtə lˈeɪə, fɔː nˈaʊ. nˈɛkst sˈiːzən, wiː ɡˌəʊ dˈiːpə.
